body:
Understanding linguistic diversity

India has a rich linguistic heritage developed through centuries of migration, settlement, trade, religious movements and cultural interaction. Its languages differ in vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, literary traditions and systems of writing.

A language family is a group of languages that developed from a common ancestral language. Linguists identify these relationships by examining systematic similarities in vocabulary, grammatical structures and sound patterns.

Languages belonging to the same family need not be mutually intelligible. Similarly, languages belonging to different families may share many words because their speakers have interacted over long periods.

A language family represents a relationship of common historical ancestry, rather than merely a geographical, religious or cultural association.

Four major language families

Most indigenous languages of India belong to 4 major linguistic families or genealogical groups: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman. Indo-Aryan is a branch of the larger Indo-European family, while Tibeto-Burman is conventionally classified within the Sino-Tibetan family.

Indo-European: Indo-Aryan branch

Indo-Aryan languages have the largest number of mother-tongue speakers in India. They are particularly widespread across northern, western, central and eastern India.

Sanskrit, Pali and the Prakrits represent important historical forms of Indo-Aryan. Modern Indo-Aryan languages include Hindi, Gujarati, Marathi, Bengali, Assamese, Punjabi, Odia, Sindhi, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Dogri, Nepali and Urdu.

Gujarati belongs to the western group of Indo-Aryan languages. Bhili and several neighbouring regional speech varieties also belong to the Indo-Aryan linguistic tradition.

Dravidian family

The Dravidian languages are concentrated mainly in southern India, although some are spoken in central and eastern India.

Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam are the 4 Dravidian languages included in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution. Other Dravidian languages include Tulu, Gondi, Kodava, Kurukh and Kui.

Tamil possesses the earliest extensive surviving literary tradition among the Dravidian languages. Dravidian languages constitute an independent language family; they are not descendants of Sanskrit, although many have absorbed Sanskrit vocabulary.

Austroasiatic family

The Austroasiatic languages of India are found mainly in parts of central and eastern India, Meghalaya and the Nicobar Islands.

  • Munda group: Santali, Mundari, Ho, Korku and several other languages.
  • Khasi: Spoken principally in Meghalaya.
  • Nicobarese languages: Spoken in the Nicobar Islands.

Santali is the only Austroasiatic language included in the Eighth Schedule.

The term Austric appears in some older classifications of Indian languages. Austroasiatic is the more precise name for the established family containing Santali, Khasi and Nicobarese.

Tibeto-Burman group

Tibeto-Burman languages are concentrated in the Himalayan region and northeastern India. Important examples include Bodo, Manipuri or Meitei, Mizo, Garo, Lepcha, Tibetan and several languages spoken by Naga communities.

Bodo and Manipuri are the 2 languages of this group included in the Eighth Schedule.

Geography does not determine language ancestry

Languages spoken in the same region need not belong to the same family. For example, Assamese belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch, Bodo belongs to the Tibeto-Burman group, and Khasi belongs to the Austroasiatic family, although all are associated with northeastern India.

The 4 major groups account for most indigenous linguistic diversity, but they do not exhaust every language spoken in India. English belongs to the Germanic branch of Indo-European, while languages such as Nihali do not have an established genealogical relationship with these major families.

Prelims focus

  • Gujarati, Assamese, Sanskrit, Pali and Urdu belong to Indo-Aryan.
  • Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam belong to the Dravidian family.
  • Santali and Khasi belong to the Austroasiatic family.
  • Bodo, Manipuri and Mizo belong to the Tibeto-Burman group.
  • Trap: Borrowing Sanskrit words does not make a Dravidian language Indo-Aryan.

[Sources: NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 1, Linguistic Classification, pp. 9–10, Table 1.2, older edition using 1991 and 2001 population data; GCERT, Class 10, Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 30–32; Census of India 2011, Language, Paper 1 of 2018, Statement 9; UNESCO, State of the Education Report for India 2025: The Mother Tongue and Multilingual Education, Chapter 3. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

title: Language Families of India

body:
Mother tongue, language and dialect

A person's mother tongue is generally the language acquired during early childhood. For Census of India 2011, the principal definition referred to the language used by the person's mother when communicating with that person during childhood. Where necessary, the language predominantly spoken in the childhood household was used.

A dialect is a variety of a language associated with a particular geographical region or social community. It may differ from other varieties in pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar.

There is no universally applicable boundary separating a language from a dialect. Mutual intelligibility, historical development, literary traditions, standardisation and community identity all influence their classification.

A standard language is a variety that has acquired widely accepted conventions for writing, grammar and formal communication. Non-standard varieties are not necessarily grammatically inferior; they follow their own linguistic patterns.

How the Census classifies languages

The Census records the names of mother tongues reported by individuals. These names require linguistic examination because different respondents may provide alternative names, local names or names of dialects belonging to the same broader language.

Census of India 2011 recorded 19,569 raw mother-tongue names. Linguistic scrutiny produced 1,369 rationalised mother tongues and identified 1,474 unclassified names, which were placed in an other-mother-tongue category.

Further classification produced a published inventory of 121 languages, comprising 22 Scheduled languages and 99 non-Scheduled languages. The report separately identified 270 classified mother tongues with at least 10,000 speakers each at the national level.

The figures 19,569, 1,369 and 121 represent different levels of Census recording and classification. They must not be treated as interchangeable counts of distinct languages.

Distribution by language family

The following percentages refer to mother-tongue speakers as a proportion of India's total population in Census 2011.

Language groupPopulation share
Indo-Aryan78.05%
Dravidian19.64%
Austroasiatic1.11%
Tibeto-Burman1.01%

The Census also separately identified the Iranian and Germanic branches of Indo-European and the Semito-Hamitic category, an older classification term used in the report. A small residual category contained other languages.

Therefore, the 4 percentages above do not represent an exhaustive distribution of every mother tongue recorded in India.

Approximately 96.71% of the population returned mother tongues classified under Scheduled languages. The remaining 3.29% belonged to other languages.

Data period and present relevance

The language report containing these figures was published on 25 June 2018 using Census 2011 data. As of 26 November 2026, Census 2027 operations were underway, but a replacement nationwide language distribution had not yet been published.

These figures describe the linguistic composition recorded in 2011. They are not estimates of India's population or language distribution in 2026.

Linguistic Survey of India

George Abraham Grierson conducted the historical Linguistic Survey of India, published between 1903 and 1928. It was a major systematic investigation of languages and dialects in British India.

The survey recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects within its coverage. Its geographical coverage and classification methods differed from those of the modern Census, so its figures cannot be directly compared with the 121 languages classified in Census 2011.

The Language Division of the Office of the Registrar General, India, established in August 1961, continues work relating to the examination and classification of Census mother-tongue returns.

Prelims focus

  • Census 2011 classified 121 languages: 22 Scheduled and 99 non-Scheduled.
  • The 2011 language report was published on 25 June 2018.
  • Indo-Aryan accounts for the largest share of mother-tongue speakers, followed by Dravidian.
  • G. A. Grierson is associated with the historical Linguistic Survey of India.
  • Trap: The raw number of mother-tongue names is not the number of independently classified languages.

[Sources: Census of India 2011, Language, Paper 1 of 2018, Introduction, pp. 2–4, and Statement 9, p. 21; Office of the Registrar General and Census Commissioner, India, Language Division; ORGI Gazette Notification on Population Enumeration, Phase 2 of Census 2027, published 2 November 2026; NCERT, Class 12, India: People and Economy, Chapter 1, Linguistic Composition, pp. 9–10, older edition. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]

body:
Language change across generations

Languages are not fixed systems. Their pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar gradually change as speakers transmit them from one generation to another. Geographical separation, migration, trade, education, political patronage and interaction with other linguistic communities contribute to these changes.

Language development does not necessarily mean that an older literary language disappears when a newer language emerges. Older and newer linguistic forms often coexist and serve different social, religious and literary purposes.

Stages of Indo-Aryan language development

The historical development of Indo-Aryan languages is conventionally divided into Old, Middle and New Indo-Aryan stages. These are broad historical categories whose boundaries overlap.

Old Indo-Aryan

Old Indo-Aryan includes Vedic Sanskrit and Classical Sanskrit.

Vedic Sanskrit is the language of the Vedic texts, including the Rigveda. The Vedic tradition was transmitted orally for long periods through carefully preserved methods of recitation.

Classical Sanskrit developed as a highly standardised literary language used in philosophy, grammar, science, religion, poetry, drama and administration.

Panini was an important Sanskrit grammarian. His work, the Ashtadhyayi, systematically describes Sanskrit grammar. He is generally placed around the middle of the first millennium BCE, although his exact date is uncertain.

Middle Indo-Aryan

Middle Indo-Aryan includes Pali, various Prakrits and later Apabhramsha varieties. These developed from earlier Indo-Aryan speech forms.

Prakrit is a collective designation for several historical Middle Indo-Aryan languages and literary varieties. It does not refer to a single uniform language.

Major Prakrit varieties include Maharashtri, Shauraseni, Magadhi and Ardhamagadhi. Prakrit languages were used in inscriptions, religious literature, poetry and drama.

Pali is an important Middle Indo-Aryan literary language. It is closely associated with the preservation of Theravada Buddhist teachings. The Pali Tipitaka consists of the Vinaya Pitaka, Sutta Pitaka and Abhidhamma Pitaka.

Ardhamagadhi Prakrit is particularly associated with the canonical literature of the Shvetambara Jain tradition. Other Jain literary traditions also employed several varieties of Prakrit, Sanskrit and Apabhramsha.

Apabhramsha refers to later Middle Indo-Aryan literary and linguistic varieties. These are important for understanding the transition towards several modern Indo-Aryan languages.

New Indo-Aryan

New Indo-Aryan languages developed gradually from regional speech varieties and became increasingly prominent in written records and literature during the medieval period.

Gujarati, Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Assamese, Punjabi and Odia belong to this stage.

It is useful to understand the broad relationship between Old Indo-Aryan, Middle Indo-Aryan and modern regional languages. However, it would be incorrect to claim that every modern Indo-Aryan language descended directly from the written form of Classical Sanskrit or from Pali.

Development of Dravidian languages

The Dravidian family followed its own historical development, independently of the Indo-Aryan sequence.

Early Tamil literature, particularly the Sangam corpus, provides important evidence of ancient Tamil language and culture. The Tolkappiyam is an early Tamil grammatical work.

Kannada, Telugu and Malayalam developed substantial literary and inscriptional traditions in their own right.

Malayalam developed in close historical relationship with Tamil in the southwestern peninsula and absorbed considerable Sanskrit influence. The Chera rulers of Mahodayapuram used Malayalam in official inscriptions from the medieval period.

The 14th-century Lilatilakam discusses grammar and poetics associated with Manipravalam, a literary tradition combining the regional language and Sanskrit.

Regional languages and medieval cultural interaction

Regional languages developed through the interaction of local speech, literary traditions, religious movements and political institutions.

The growing use of Persian in administration during the Delhi Sultanate and Mughal periods introduced many Persian and Arabic-derived words into Indian languages. Regional languages nevertheless continued to develop.

In Bengal, for example, Persian served administrative functions while Bengali expanded as a literary language. Bengali absorbed vocabulary from Sanskrit, regional languages, Persian and later European languages.

The Bhakti movement also encouraged the use of regional languages because devotional compositions and teachings could reach wider sections of society.

A language can develop independently while borrowing vocabulary and literary forms from another language. Language contact and common linguistic ancestry are different processes.

Prelims focus

  • Panini: Ashtadhyayi and Sanskrit grammar.
  • Pali: Middle Indo-Aryan and Theravada Buddhist literature.
  • Ardhamagadhi: Shvetambara Jain canonical tradition.
  • Apabhramsha: later Middle Indo-Aryan varieties.
  • Tolkappiyam: early Tamil grammar.
  • Trap: Dravidian languages did not develop through the Sanskrit–Prakrit–Apabhramsha sequence.

[Sources: GCERT, Class 10, Social Science, Gujarati-medium edition, Chapter 4, Literary Heritage of India, pp. 30–33; NCERT, Class 7, Our Pasts II, 2020–21 edition, Chapter 9, The Making of Regional Cultures, pp. 122–123 and 130–132; Census of India, The Written Languages of the World: A Survey of the Degree and Modes of Use, Constitutional Languages, India, Gujarati section, p. 123; Press Information Bureau, Classical Languages of India, 27 October 2025. Online sources consulted on 26 November 2026.]
